Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:46: And when he suffers a financial loss in a matter that does not involve his fellow — such as his ship being wrecked and the like — he should accept the judgment of Heaven with love, and think of what Job said (Job 1:21), "naked I came out of my mother's womb." We have seen fit to explain some of the words of this verse, according to our limited understanding, because of the benefit for practical life that follows from it. The matter of "naked I came out" is to indicate that a person has no connection or relation to his money at all — for just as he came into this world naked of all wealth, so he will return to his grave naked of the wealth of the world; and the word "shamah" [there] is, according to the plain sense, imprecise, but according to the secret it is precise, good, and fitting, and there is no room here to elaborate on its secret. Here, then, is one argument that one should not be concerned over the loss of money, for in the end he must inevitably leave it behind, and it neither raises nor lowers the benefit to his soul. And should you say, money is good for one who merits it, since he has the ability to do good to the poor, to students of Torah, to widows and orphans — to this the verse answers, "the LORD gave and the LORD has taken away" — for when He gave it to him, He gave it with the attribute of mercy, and when He took it, He and His court took it; and if it had seemed to Him and His court that the money was good for him and for his soul, He would not have taken it from him. Further, he intends by saying "the LORD gave" — for why should a person complain about what is not his own? This is "the LORD gave," and everything is from His hand, as King David, peace be upon him, said (1 Chronicles 29:14), "for everything is from You, and from Your hand we have given You." "And the LORD has taken away" — to indicate that a person should not complain about the deed of the supernal court, which is the LORD Himself, for "righteousness and justice are the foundation of His throne" — shall the clay say to its Potter, what are You doing? "Blessed be the name of the LORD" — for a person is obligated to bless over the bad just as he blesses over the good (Berachot 9:5), the reason being that His judgments toward us are for our own good, to purify our souls, as He says (Psalms 145:9), "the LORD is good to all, and His mercies are over all His works." For this reason Nachum Ish Gam Zu used to say "gam zu letovah" ["this too is for the good"] (Ta'anit 21a), and my teacher, peace be upon him, explained "gam zu" — even though it is judgment [din], it is for the good [tovah], which is Chesed — to bind judgment always with love, which is Chesed; and this too is "blessed be the name of the LORD," for blessing is on the right side (Zohar, portion Ki Tisa, 192a).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:47: Further, among the ruinous consequences that flow from anger, it is written in the Book of Qualities found among us in manuscript (Orchot Tzaddikim, ch. 12): the first, that if he is a teacher of students, because of his anger the students fear to ask him about their difficulties, lest he become angry with them; and even if they do ask, he does not explain to his students all that is needed, but answers them in an angry manner, and through this they do not understand — this is what is meant (Avot 2:5), "and an exacting person cannot teach."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:48: The angry person has no favor in the eyes of people, and is like a fool in their eyes, and therefore his deeds are not accepted in people's eyes — even if he has Torah and good deeds, no one learns from him. Rav Safra expounded, an irritable person gains nothing from his hand but his own irritability (cf. Kiddushin, end of 40b). The angry person does not overlook his own way and does not forgive his own affront, but always bears a grudge and takes revenge. Anger brings a person to strife, for when he is angry at his fellows, they quarrel with him and he with them, and when there is strife, then those who hate him envy him — you already know the evil of strife, as will be explained at the time of [discussing] strife.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:49: The angry person withholds his heart from all good, for when he is angry he has no heart to have mercy on the poor — for of the Name it is said (Habakkuk 3:2), "in wrath remember mercy," and this is far from the ways of people. Anger nullifies a person's heart in prayer, and they said the Shechinah does not rest amid anger, for no angry person will ever be a great sage, since anger drives wisdom from his heart so that he cannot answer properly nor rebuke properly, and all his words are without sense.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:50: The angry person is deprived of moral instruction and rebuke, for no one is permitted to reveal to him his mistakes and his disgraceful ways, since everyone refrains from telling him of his own matters lest he become angry at them; and even if people do rebuke him, he does not accept their words because of his anger. In sum, an angry person accepts no good quality unless he removes anger from his heart.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:51: Just as the angry person does not accept rebuke from others, so he cannot rebuke others — for the Torah says (Leviticus 19:17), "you shall surely rebuke your fellow and not bear sin because of him" — begin the rebuke calmly and privately, speaking to him in a soft and pleading tongue, showing that you speak for his own good, and then you will not bear sin because of him; but if you rebuke your fellow with a loud, angry voice, then you will bear sin because of him, for he will be embarrassed, and that fellow will not accept the rebuke — for such is the way of people: when a person comes upon his fellow forcefully, his fellow hardens against him and does not submit to him. Regarding this Solomon said (Ecclesiastes 9:17), "the words of the wise, spoken gently, are heard." You already know of Hillel and Shammai — Shammai was exacting and Hillel was humble; they said, converts came [saying]: the exactingness of Shammai sought to drive us from the world, but the humility of Hillel drew us near under the wings of the Shechinah (Shabbat 31a). Because of Hillel's great humility, no one could anger him, for whoever restrains himself from anger acquires the attribute of humility and compassion, since from the wrath of the LORD's anger immediately comes cruelty, as it is written (Exodus 22:23), "and My anger shall burn, and I will kill you with the sword"; therefore vengeance is always written alongside burning anger, as it is written (Deuteronomy 11:17), "and the LORD's anger shall burn against you, and He will shut up the heavens" etc., and there are many such cases.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:52: Anger causes brazenness in a person, for out of anger he will not submit nor admit the truth. And the sage said, when you wish to test whether to associate with a person, anger him — if he admits the truth to you at the time of his anger, then associate with him; if not, leave him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:53: Anger brings a person to error, for who was greater than Moses, who became angry in three places and came to error? As it is said, "and Moses was angry with them," and it is written (Leviticus 10:16), "and he was angry with Elazar and with Itamar," and it is written (ibid. 10:17), "why have you not eaten the sin-offering" [implying he forgot the reason and needed correction]. And it is written (Numbers 20:10), "listen now, you rebels" etc., and it is written (ibid. 20:11), "and he struck the rock" [instead of speaking to it as commanded]. And it is written (Numbers 31:14), "and Moses was angry with the officers of the army," and it is written after it (ibid. 31:21), "and Elazar the priest said, this is the statute of the law" — teaching that the halakhah had been forgotten by Moses. Now you can understand: if this happened to Moses, who was the father of the sages, how much more so will it happen to fools every day; therefore Solomon said (Ecclesiastes 7:9), "do not hasten in your spirit to be angry."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:54: Be very careful that no ruinous act occur in the midst of anger, for our Sages of blessed memory said (Shabbat 105b), whoever tears his garments, breaks his vessels, or scatters his money in his rage, should be in your eyes like one who worships idols, for such is the craft of the evil inclination — today it tells him to do this, and tomorrow it tells him to do such and such and worship idols, and he worships — as it is written (Psalms 81:10), "there shall be no foreign god within you" — and what is this foreign god within a person's body? Say, this is the evil inclination that incites a person at the time of his anger.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:55: Our Sages of blessed memory said (Avot 5:11): four types of temperament exist: easily angered and easily appeased — his loss is offset by his gain; hard to appease and hard to anger — his gain is offset by his loss; easily angered and hard to appease — this is wicked; hard to anger and easily appeased — this is pious. These four qualities are said of the righteous, when they become angry over good matters or worldly affairs; but easily angered against transgressors and easily appeased toward them is a bad quality, since he becomes reconciled to the wicked — and all the more so one who is easily angered against the righteous, and hard to anger against the wicked, easily appeased toward the wicked and hard to appease toward the righteous — this is a completely wicked person.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:56: Although anger is a very bad quality, nevertheless a person must at times conduct himself with the quality of anger — such as to discipline the wicked, to cast fear upon the members of his household, and to instill awe in his students. And when he is angry against transgressors, he should weigh his anger as though on a scale — for Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, said of Reuven and Gad (Numbers 32:14), "a brood of sinful men" — therefore his own grandson became a priest for idols; and even though he was angry for the sake of Heaven, a good measure is needed in all of a person's ways, and he should see how to make it a mitzvah, whether in his anger or in his laughter. A person who has the quality of anger and forces his temperament and conduct as though he were not angry and not one prone to anger — of him it is said (Proverbs 16:32), "better slow to anger than a mighty man" — and "slow to anger" is one of the thirteen attributes said of the Holy One, blessed be He.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:57: The sage said, one whose anger comes upon him through thought will show settled judgment; one whose anger comes upon him without thought will show foolishness. They further said, one who is intensely angry and irritable is not far from the raging insane; and one who is habitually angry has no true life and is never happy, and since he is not happy, he does not accept any of his circumstances with joy, does not justify the judgment upon himself, and cannot serve the Name, blessed be He, with joy. When a person is fasting, or in some other distress, anger is then present in his heart; therefore at these times he must be especially careful not to become angry. Silence nullifies anger, as does a lowered voice; therefore when a person sees his anger growing stronger, he should remain silent or speak calmly and not raise his voice in his anger, for raising one's voice at a time of anger arouses the anger further, but a lowered voice and silence calm the anger. Also, he should not look at the face of the person he is angry at, but speak to him without looking at his face, and this will drive the anger from his heart.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:58: Know that a person's perfection is when he rules over his anger, as it is said (Proverbs 19:11), "the intelligence of a man makes him slow to anger." Anger tends strongly toward pride, and you already know the evils of pride. It is fitting for a person to distance himself from anger even regarding something over which it would be fitting to be angry — nevertheless, he should restrain his spirit and not become angry. One prone to anger must first, when he decides not to become angry, work so that he feels nothing at all — even if he is rebuked and cursed, he should not respond, should not become angry, and should not care. This is a clear matter: for one who was very exacting, it is easier for him not to feel anything at all and remain completely silent and restrain his spirit entirely, than for him to become slightly angry — for the angry person cannot do this, since if he allows a little anger into his heart, in the end it becomes much.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:59: One who wants to restrain his spirit from anger, yet wants to cast fear upon the members of his household, or, if he is a communal leader, wants to be angry with the community to bring them back to the right path — how should he do it? He should show himself before them as though he were angry, in order to discipline them, while his mind remains settled within himself alone — like a person who displays anger at the time of his anger but is not [truly] angry. And when he displays his anger toward the members of his household, he should be careful not to do so when there are poor guests present, since they might think he is angry at them; therefore he should show himself joyful before them.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:60: The Sages commanded distancing oneself from anger to the point of training oneself not to feel even things that would anger, until anger is uprooted from the heart entirely — and this is the good path and the way of the righteous, for they are insulted and do not insult, hear their own disgrace and do not respond, rejoice in sufferings and justify the judgment upon themselves; of them the verse says (Judges 5:31), "and those who love Him are like the sun going forth in its might."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:1: Although in the preceding chapter we explained the causes that nullify anger, and it might have appeared at first glance that the nullification of anger alone suffices for acquiring humility — since from the negative you infer the positive — nevertheless one must know that acquiring humility requires many things, for there are levels, as proven by the verse (Proverbs 22:4), "the heel of humility is the fear of the LORD" — meaning, the final level of humility is the fear of the LORD, just as the heel is the final part of a person's body; and since this is so, there are many levels to it requiring explanation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:2: The first step in acquiring humility is that a person train himself to acquire the four qualities mentioned in the Mishnah in tractate Avot, at the beginning of the chapter of Ben Zoma (4:1): who is wise? He who learns from every person. Who is mighty? He who conquers his inclination. Who is rich? He who is happy with his portion. Who is honored? He who honors the creatures, etc. These four qualities correspond to the four letters of the Name, and with a little examination, the reader familiar with the words of Rashbi, peace be upon him, will know how these designations correctly apply, each to its own place. Regarding humility, without doubt one who learns from every person is certainly humble, for out of his great humility he is not concerned about learning Torah even from the smallest of the small, since he cares only for the honor of Torah — this is (Psalms 119:99), "for Your testimonies are my meditation." And so it is said in the Zohar (portion Acharei Mot, 69a), that it is taught: whoever heeds words of Torah is fortunate in this world, as though he had received Torah from Sinai — and even from every person he must listen to words of Torah; and whoever bends his ear toward him gives honor to the Holy King and gives honor to Torah, and of him it is written (Deuteronomy 27:9), "this day you have become a people to the LORD your God."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:3: Who is mighty? He who conquers his inclination — as explained, "better slow to anger than a mighty man," for if they disgrace and anger him, he will be slow to anger and conquer his inclination and remain silent — this is the true mighty one, and he is better than the mighty one called mighty in battle. Regarding the proof, it is possible to say that the proof from the verse is that since the verse says "better slow to anger than a mighty man," one only says "better this than that" if they fall within the same category — showing that one slow to anger is also mighty, and deserves to be called mighty since he performs greater might in conquering his inclination than the mighty one who conquers battles of nations. This is one of the qualities of humility — being slow to anger — and he is called mighty for conquering his inclination, because the inclination is drawn downward from the dross of gold, and he conquers it and gives it no room to spread, along the lines of what is explained in Tikkunim (12a), that this is like a dog restrained by a chain.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:4: Who is rich? He who is happy with his portion — for among the qualities of humility is being content with little, as explained in the first chapter of this gate, that this is one of the qualities of Abraham our father, peace be upon him: a good eye, a humble spirit, etc. (5:19); and whoever pursues luxuries becomes proud of heart, as it is written (Deuteronomy 8:12), "lest you eat and be satisfied, and build good houses and dwell in them... and your heart become proud and you forget the LORD your God" (ibid. 8:14).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:5: Who is honored? He who honors the creatures — this too is among the qualities of humility, to honor all creatures, whether poor or rich, since all are made in the supernal image; whoever honors them honors the Craftsman who made them, and whoever, God forbid, disgraces them, disgraces the Craftsman. As they said in Ta'anit (20b) regarding Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, who said, how ugly is this man! [The man] said to him, go tell the craftsman who made me how ugly is this vessel You have made, until he had to ask him for forgiveness, and he said to him, I forgive you, forgive me, etc. — this is the same as the statement in Bereshit Rabbah that we copied in the preceding chapter, on the verse "this is the book of the generations of man"; see there. And in honoring every person, whether small or great, this applies except toward the proud, for the proud person shows in his soul that honor befits him and that other people are lesser in his eyes and he does not honor them. His proof is the verse (1 Samuel 2:30), "for those who honor Me I will honor" — and Rabbeinu Ovadiah, peace be upon him, explained "for those who honor Me I will honor" as a kal vachomer: if the Holy One, blessed be He, who is the King of Glory, and everything He created in His world He created only for His own honor, honors those who honor Him, how much more so should flesh and blood [honor those who honor them]. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:6: Close to the interpretation I have given, I found that the pious Rabbi Yosef Yavetz, peace be upon him, explained, these are his words: know that these four levels comprise the entire perfection of man. The first is the level of wisdom; the second and third are levels of action — the second being negative commandments, and the third, action [positive], as they said (Berachot 8a), greater is one who benefits from his own labor than one who fears Heaven, as I have already mentioned. And the fourth is the most excellent of all, when all are brought to perfection — for when they all combine and unite in complete unity, then humility, which is greater than all the [other] merits, is unified from among them — as they said (Avodah Zarah 20b), humility is greater than all of them, and it is what brings one to the holy spirit; and it is written (Proverbs 16:32... rather 18:12, but as cited in source), "and before honor comes humility." Therefore Ben Zoma called him "honored," for the honor of the LORD hovers over him all day and rests between his shoulders, and these [qualities] draw one another along. For wisdom — one who knows the worth of his own soul and its measure will not sell it for momentary pleasure — a parable of two men who each had two fine pearls: the one who knows the pearl's worth guards it like the pupil of his eye, while the one who does not know its worth will give it away for a loaf of bread. So too, the boorish do not feel the worth of their own soul and therefore send themselves into transgressions, but the wise man, concerned about his soul, will guard it, and the fear of Heaven will come into his heart — wisdom, by its power, weakens the power of the evil inclination, and from the side of fear, the power of love begins to sparkle within him, for fear and love, both bound as one, join together and do not separate; and also, from his conquering his inclination, he is content with little and is pleased to give his tithe to whoever he has entrusted with it — and behold, one who does good to people with his money, all the more so with the sweetness of his tongue. We find, then, that these four merits draw one another along. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:7: Now, along the lines of "who is honored" that the aforementioned pious author, peace be upon him, explained as being the secret of supernal honor, and it is likewise so according to my own way — this helps us understand what they said in Eruvin (13b), these are their words, regarding the question of why they merited establishing the halakhah like Beit Hillel: because they were pleasant and humble, teaching that whoever lowers himself, the Holy One, blessed be He, raises him up, and whoever raises himself, the Holy One, blessed be He, lowers him; and whoever pursues greatness, greatness flees from him, and whoever flees from greatness, greatness pursues him; and whoever pushes his moment [i.e., forces his fortune], the moment pushes him away, and whoever is pushed aside because of the moment, the moment stands ready for him. Thus far his words. And Rashi, peace be upon him, explained: "pushes his moment" — one who strains to grow rich and become great and sees that he is not succeeding, yet nevertheless returns and travels far and thrusts himself into lofty positions. "The moment stands ready" — after some time, a successful moment is destined to stand ready for him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:8: The reason that whoever lowers himself, the Holy One, blessed be He, raises him up, and the rest of the statement, is as we explained in the first chapter of this gate — that the Shechinah rests only upon a broken and crushed heart, and the poor, who are her broken vessels (Zohar, portion Vayikra, 9a), are her throne, as it says (Isaiah 57:15), "I dwell in the high and holy place, and with the crushed and humble of spirit." And we explained in the Gate of Repentance (ch. 4) that as the moon fills and renews itself, those attached to it renew themselves and rise with it; and one who does the opposite has his spirit become proud, and the Shechinah distances itself from him, and then greatness also flees from him — for when the Holy One, blessed be He, is pleased with a person and rests upon him, He gives him favor in people's eyes, that they honor and exalt him; but when the Holy One, blessed be He, is not with him, people too distance themselves from him, along the lines of "anyone with whom the spirit of the Omnipresent is pleased, the spirit of the creatures is pleased with him" etc. (Avot 3:10); therefore, "when the LORD is pleased with a man's ways, He makes even his enemies to be at peace with him" (Proverbs 16:7). Along these lines, [greatness] is called "gedulah" from the side of greatness, and is called "the hour" [sha'ah], as explained in Tikkunim, these designations for her — and therefore the secret of supernal greatness flees from him, and likewise the moment pushes him away, or the moment stands ready for him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:9: Through this several verses in Proverbs regarding humility are understood. The first (Proverbs 15:33), "and before honor comes humility" — meaning, before the supernal honor rests upon a person, he must be humble, for the reason stated. Likewise (ibid. 29:23), "and one humble of spirit shall attain honor" — for through humility of spirit one becomes a throne for the Shechinah and supports her, like a chair that supports a person. Likewise (ibid. 20:3), "it is an honor for a man to cease from strife" — meaning, the drawing of supernal honor to a man is when he ceases from strife; but if he is a man of strife and quarrel, supernal honor flees from him. Therefore, in order to merit the level of supernal honor, one must grasp all the qualities of humility found explained in the verses and in the Gemara.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:10: Besides what has been explained in the preceding chapters, we find further conditions, and these are they. First, submission in all his worldly matters, both revealed and hidden, in his speech, his deeds, and the movement of his limbs and their power, so that his inner self not be the opposite of his outer appearance, nor his hidden self against his revealed self; and his movements should be balanced, correct, and consistent, proceeding along the path of submission and lowliness toward God, blessed be He, and toward people, according to the differences in their levels, and according to what is good for him from them, for his Torah and his world, as it is said (Psalms 112:5), "good is the man who is gracious and lends, who conducts his affairs with justice," and the Sages said (Avot 4:10), be humble of spirit before every person, and they said (3:12), be quick [to greet] every person and gracious to all. Thus far from Chovot HaLevavot (Gate of Submission, ch. 6).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:11: Of this category is what they said in Sanhedrin (88b): they sent from there [the land of Israel], who is a son of the World to Come? One who is humble and lowly of stature, who bows down when entering and bows down when leaving, and constantly studies Torah, and does not take credit for himself — the Sages fixed their eyes upon Rav Ulla bar Abba [as fitting this description]. Thus far his words. And Rashi, peace be upon him, explained "shayf": he bends low entering and bends low leaving, etc.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:12: Further, at the end, it was Abaye's constant saying (Berachot 17a): a person should always be cunning in fear [of Heaven], answer gently to turn away wrath, and increase peace with his brothers, his relatives, and every person, even with a gentile in the marketplace, so that he be beloved above and cherished below and accepted by the creatures. They said of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai that no person ever greeted him first, even a gentile in the marketplace. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:13: And likewise we learn in Avot, chapter 4 (4:15): Rabbi Matya ben Charash says, be quick to greet every person, and be a tail to lions rather than a head to foxes. He explained the reason for "be a tail to lions rather than a head to foxes" — for the tail of a lion is called a lion, while the head of a fox is a fox.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:14: Likewise, among the conditions of lowliness is being among the disciples of Aaron, loving peace and pursuing peace (Avot 1:12), which is explained in the beraita of tractate Kallah (ch. 3) — that humility of spirit is learned from Aaron, as it is written (Malachi 2:7), "for the priest's lips shall guard knowledge" — and there is no one more humble of spirit than one who pursues peace; and consider in your mind how one pursues peace if he is not humble of spirit — how so? If a person curses him, he says to him, "peace be with you"; if a person quarrels with him, he remains silent. Further, if two are quarreling, he humbles his spirit and goes to one, appeasing him regarding the other, and likewise to the other — such was Aaron's craft, and the manner of the pursuit of peace that Aaron practiced is explained there and copied in Menorat HaMaor of Rabbi Yitzchak Aboab, peace be upon him (Ner 6, Rule 2, ch. 2), and therefore we shall not elaborate further in copying his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:15: Further, under this category of submission is that when he sits among people, he should choose the lowest of places for himself, and so they said in Vayikra Rabbah (1:5): Rabbi Yehoshua of Sikhnin in the name of Rabbi Levi opened the verse (Proverbs 25:7), "for it is better that it be said to you, come up here, than that you be humbled before a noble." Rabbi Akiva teaches it in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Azzai: distance yourself from your place two or three seats and sit until they say to you, come up here, and do not sit up close so they will say to you, go down — better that they say to you, go up, go up, than that they say to you, go down, go down. And so Hillel says, my lowering is my raising, my raising is my lowering — what is the reason? "He who raises Himself up to sit, He who lowers Himself" (Psalms 113:5-6). You find that at the time the Holy One, blessed be He, revealed Himself to Moses from within the thornbush, Moses hid his face from Him, as it is said (Exodus 3:6), "and Moses hid his face" — the Holy One, blessed be He, said to him (ibid. 3:10), "come, and I will send you to Pharaoh" [raising him up because he lowered himself]. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:16: Further, they said in the Midrash Mechilta (Bachodesh 3): Rabbi Yosi says, a place does not honor a man, but a man honors his place; from here they said, as long as the Shechinah rested on the mountain (Exodus 19:12), "whoever touches the mountain shall surely die" — once the Shechinah departed, everyone was permitted to go up the mountain. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:17: Likewise, under this category of aspect is that a person should minimize his own affairs, as they expounded in Bereshit Rabbah (6:4): why was he named Yaktan ["the small one"]? Because he made himself and his affairs small — and what did he merit? He merited to establish thirteen families. And if the small one, who minimized his own affairs [merited this], how much more so a great one who minimizes his affairs. Similarly (Genesis 48:14), "and Israel stretched out his right hand and placed it on Ephraim's head, though he was the younger" — Rabbi Chananya said, do we not already know from the genealogy that he was the younger? Rather, it means he minimized his own affairs — and what did he merit? He merited the birthright. If the younger one merited the birthright through minimizing his affairs, how much more so a greater one who minimizes his affairs.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:18: Further, regarding the merit of one who minimizes himself, it is explained in the Zohar (portion Shelach Lecha, 168a) — these are novel teachings that the souls of the righteous told Rashbi, peace be upon him, from the academy above. These are his words: ah, Rabbi, how many new words from the great academy! Fortunate is one who makes himself small in this world — how great and supernal he is in that world; and so the head of the academy opened: whoever is small is great, and whoever is great is small, as it is written (Genesis 23:1), "and the life of Sarah was a hundred years and twenty years and seven years" — a hundred, which is a great number, is written with "year" [in the singular, as though small]; the smallness of years — one — he made it small; seven, which is a small number, he enlarged and made it great, as it is written "seven years" [plural]. Come and see, the Holy One, blessed be He, makes great only him who makes himself small, and makes small only him who makes himself great — fortunate is one who makes himself small in this world, how great he becomes in exaltation in that world. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:19: Likewise our Sages of blessed memory expounded in Megillat Esther on the verse (Ezekiel 21:31), "remove the turban": Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said, "remove the turban" — whoever is great in this world is small in the World to Come. Rabbi Miyasha bar Miyasha, grandson of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, was silent during his illness for three days; after three days his mind settled upon him. His father said to him, where were you, my son? He said to him, I was in a confused world. What did you see there? He said, I saw many people — here in honor and there in disgrace, there in honor and here in disgrace. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:20: Further, among the conditions of humility is to receive every person with joy, a pleasant countenance, and to greet every person first; and if he speaks with his fellow, he should not speak with an angry face but with a smiling face — and our Sages of blessed memory explained in Ketubot (111b) on the verse (Genesis 49:12), "and white [white teeth] with milk" — these are their words: Rabbi said, it is better to whiten one's teeth [smile] toward one's fellow than to give him milk to drink, as it is said, "and white teeth" — do not read "livnon" [white] but "libbun" [whitening] of teeth. Thus far their words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:21: Likewise, he should not refrain from speaking and responding first to first, even to the smallest of the small, and this is learned from the story of Hillel the Elder, brought in Shabbat, chapter 2 (31a), where a man said to Hillel, "sit," and he would respond to every single matter, and did not say, "I have no time now, come tomorrow," or other such postponements. Similarly we find with Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, whom a certain child called and he walked after him a distance of three miles, as is stated in the Midrash and copied in the Yalkut, Isaiah (§478), on the verse (Isaiah 54:12), "and I will make your suns of rubies" [read as "your gates"].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:22: Further, among the conditions of humility, he wrote in Chovot HaLevavot (Gate of Submission, ch. 6), that one should do good to people, speak good of them, judge them favorably, not speak of their disgrace, and forgive them for what they say and speak in his own disgrace, even if they are not deserving of forgiveness. Regarding forgiving evil and disgraceful speech, the verse says (Numbers 12:1), "and Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses," and it says (ibid. 12:3), "and the man Moses was very humble" — because he forgave them; and he said (Psalms 7:5), "if I have repaid evil to him who was at peace with me" [i.e., he did not]; and it says (Proverbs 24:29), "do not say, as he has done to me, so I will do to him." Our Sages of blessed memory said (Gittin 36b), those who are insulted and do not insult, who hear their own disgrace and do not respond, who act out of love and rejoice in sufferings — of them the verse says (Judges 5:31), "and those who love Him are like the sun going forth in its might." Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:23: What follows from this is that he should not hand over judgment against his fellow [i.e., invoke divine judgment upon him], as we learn at the end of the chapter "HaChovel" (Bava Kama 93a): Rabbi Yochanan said, whoever hands over judgment against his fellow is himself punished first, as it is said (Genesis 16:5), "and Sarai said to Abram, my wrong be upon you," and it is written (ibid. 23:2), "and Abraham came to mourn for Sarah and to weep for her" [i.e., she was punished with death first] — and this applies when he has no [recourse to a human] judge on earth. Rabbi Yitzchak said, woe to the one who cries out [invoking divine judgment], more than to the one cried out against — it was likewise taught: both the one who cries out and the one cried out against are implied [in being subject to divine scrutiny], but they hasten [punishment] against the one who cries out more than against the one cried out against. Thus far his words. And Rashi explained: both the one who cries out and the one cried out against are implied — "and My anger shall burn, and I will kill you [plural]" (Exodus 22:23) implies two — but they hasten against the crier first, as we find with Sarah. Thus far his words. I heard the reason for this from my teacher, peace be upon him: it is not fitting to arouse judgment above, for the King should always be in a good disposition toward all; and one who hands over judgment arouses accusation and judgment above, and the King becomes angry to execute judgment, as it is written (Proverbs 16:14), "the wrath of a king is like messengers of death"; therefore they exact payment from the crier first, since he aroused the judgment that had been quiet — along the lines of (Ecclesiastes 10:8), "whoever digs a pit shall fall into it." For this reason Mar Zutra used to say every night before sleeping, "I forgive whoever has distressed me," as we say in Megillah, chapter "Bnei Ha'ir" (28a), "nor did my fellow's curse ever ascend upon my bed" — for so did Mar Zutra do: when he went up to his bed he would say, "I forgive whoever has distressed me." Thus far his words — so that he not be the cause of arousing judgment to afflict any creature. This is the quality of the pious, which is beyond the letter of the law — for even though he was not crying out about a matter that had no [recourse to] judgment below, so that he would have been permitted to cry out, he would nevertheless forgive.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:24: Likewise, it is fitting to be careful not to provoke one's fellow, lest a mishap occur, for sometimes the curse of an ordinary person is fulfilled, as we learn there (Bava Kama 93a), these are their words: and Rabbi Yitzchak said, a person should never consider the curse of an ordinary person light in his eyes, for Avimelech cursed Sarah, and it was fulfilled in her offspring, as it is said (Genesis 20:16), "behold, it is for you a covering of the eyes" — he said to her, since you covered from me and did not reveal that he is your husband, and caused me this distress, may it be [God's] will that you have children whose eyes are covered — and it was fulfilled in her offspring, as it is written (ibid. 27:1), "and it came to pass, when Isaac was old, that his eyes became too dim to see." Thus far his words. And further there, Rabbi Abahu said, a person should always be among the pursued rather than among the pursuers, for there is no bird more pursued than turtledoves and young pigeons, and yet the verse deemed them fit for the altar. Thus far his words.
